title: Chapter 3: The Intractable 1
content:
Chapter 3

The Intractable 1

Wei Wuxian had originally intended to wash his face and catch a glimpse of whatever features his host had left behind. But the room didn’t have a single drop of water—none to drink, none to wash with.

The only basin-like container in sight looked far more suited for taking a piss than washing up.

He gave the door a shove, but it was bolted tight from the outside. Apparently, they were dead set on keeping him from wandering off.

Not one damn thing about this rebirth was bringing him any joy!

Figuring he had nowhere else to go, he settled into a meditative stance to let his soul sync with the new vessel. He sat like that for an entire day. By the time he opened his eyes, thin ribbons of sunlight were slicing through the cracks in the door and window frames. He could stand and walk now, sure, but his skull was still throbbing and his vision swam just as badly as before. Wei Wuxian frowned to himself: Mo Xuanyu’s cultivation is laughably negligible, but there’s no reason my soul shouldn’t be able to pilot a mortal shell this weak. Why does this body feel like such dead weight?

It wasn't until his gut let out an ungodly rumble that the truth hit him. It had nothing to do with cultivation or spiritual energy—the body simply hadn't reached the inedia stage, and it was starving to death. If he didn't hunt down a meal soon, he was going to go down in history as the very first vengeful spirit to be summoned from the grave only to starve right back into it.

Sucking in a breath, Wei Wuxian wound up to kick the door off its hinges. Before his foot could connect, heavy footsteps shuffled up outside. Someone gave the panel a rough boot, barking impatiently, “Chow time!”

The shout was loud enough, but the door never budged. Wei Wuxian glanced down and saw a flap swing open near the bottom—a hatch barely big enough to shove a battered bowl through. It slammed onto the dirt floor right in front of him.

The servant outside snapped, “Hurry it up! Stop dragging your feet and slide the bowl back out when you're done!”

The dog-flap was too cramped for any person to squeeze through, but just wide enough to haul a bowl inside. It held a meager portion of cold rice flanked by two unidentifiable, greasy side dishes. Wei Wuxian poked at the mismatched chopsticks stabbed upright in the grain, feeling a wave of tragic self-pity wash over him:

The great Yiling Laozu returns to the mortal realm, only to get kicked around, cussed out, and greeted with a welcome feast of literal slops. Where were the rivers of blood? The ruthless slaughter? The ruined clans? If he told anyone, they’d laugh him right out of the room. Talk about a tiger stranded in the shallows getting bullied by stray mutts, or a plucked phoenix being treated worse than a scrawny chicken.

Just then, the voice outside piped up again, though this time dripping with sleazy charm: “A-Ding! Over here, gorgeous.”

A sweet, lilting girl's voice answered from across the courtyard. “A-Tong? You’re stuck bringing slops to that freak again?”

A-Tong spat loudly. “Why else would I step foot in this cursed yard!”

Her footsteps drew closer until she stopped right outside the door. “You only deliver food once a day, and you slack off half the time without anyone giving you hell. You’ve got it easy and you still complain. Look at me! I'm buried in so many chores I can't even slip out to have any fun.”

A-Tong whined, “Hey, feeding him isn’t my only job! Besides, would you even dare sneak out lately? With all those walking corpses shuffling around, every household in the village has their gates barred tight.”

Wei Wuxian squatted against the door, shovel-feeding cold rice into his mouth with the uneven chopsticks, listening intently.

It sounded like Mo Village had hit a rough patch. Walking corpses—literally what the name implied, dead men walking—were the bottom-feeders of the undead world. Dull-eyed and sluggish, their combat threat was practically zero, but they were still plenty terrifying to ordinary folk. The sheer stench of rot alone was enough to make a mortal heave their guts out.

To Wei Wuxian, however, they were the most compliant, easy-to-herd puppets on the market. Hearing about them now felt almost nostalgic.

A-Tong’s voice dropped into a greasy murmur. “Tell you what, if you really want to go out, bring me along. I’ll keep you safe…”

A-Ding scoffed. “You? Protect me? Don't flatter yourself. As if you could take down one of those monsters!”

A-Tong grumbled defensively, “Well, if I can’t beat them, neither can anyone else in this town!”

A-Ding laughed. “Who says nobody can? Let me tell you, cultivators from the immortal sects arrived in Mo Village today! I heard they’re from a ridiculously prestigious clan, too! Madam is entertaining them in the main hall right now, and half the town has crowded the courtyard just to gawk. Hear that noise? Sounds like a riot out east. I don't have time to mess around with you—Madam’s going to order me around any second.”

Wei Wuxian perked his ears. Sure enough, a distant murmur of voices drifted over from the eastern wing. He chewed the thought over for two seconds, hauled himself up, and planted a solid kick against the door.

Crack. The wooden bolt snapped clean in half.

The two servants, still caught mid-flirtation, screeched at the top of their lungs as the double doors blew wide open. Wei Wuxian tossed the wooden bowl aside and stepped outside into the courtyard. The afternoon sunlight hit him like a blinding wall, making his eyes sting and his pale skin prickle. He raised a forearm over his brow, blinking through the glare.

A-Tong had shrieked even louder than the girl, but the moment he realized the intruder was just the town’s resident punching bag, his courage flared back up. Desperate to save face in front of A-Ding, he bounded forward, shooing at Wei Wuxian like he was an annoying stray. “Scram! Back inside! What the hell do you think you’re doing out here?!”

People treated mangy dogs and flies with more dignity. It was obvious how the servants usually handled Mo Xuanyu; because the poor soul had never fought back, they took every liberty they pleased. Wei Wuxian casually hooked his foot behind the servant’s ankle, sending A-Tong sprawling in a graceless heap on the dirt.

He offered a bright, eerie grin. “And who the hell do you think you’re bossing around?”

Leaving the dazed boy on the ground, Wei Wuxian followed the commotion straight toward the eastern courtyard. The main hall was packed three layers deep with locals crane-necking for a look. The moment Wei Wuxian crossed the threshold of the outer yard, a woman’s shrill, overbearing voice rose over the chatter:

“…We have a junior in our own family, you see, who was once graced by an immortal bond…”

Ah. Madam Mo was shamelessly fishing for a connection with the sect disciples.

Before she could finish her pitch, Wei Wuxian threw elbows through the crowd, barreling straight into the main hall while waving frantically. “I’m here, I’m here! Right over here!”

Seated prominently at the head of the room was a well-kept, middle-aged woman draped in lavish silk—Madam Mo herself. Her live-in husband sat meekly at her side, a clear step down in authority. Seated across from them were several teenage boys clad in flowing white robes, swords slung across their backs.

The sudden intrusion of a wild-eyed, disheveled lunatic brought the entire room to a dead, suffocating halt. Wei Wuxian, oblivious to the horrified silence, beamed with utter shamelessness. “Who called for me? The one blessed with immortal fate—that's me, isn't it?!”

He’d caked on so much cheap powder that the broad smile cracked the makeup, sending little white flakes fluttering to the floor like snow. Across the room, one of the white-robed boys let out a muffled snort, almost choking on his laughter, until a sharp glare from the boy sitting at their head forced him back into rigid posture.

Wei Wuxian let his gaze flick across the youths, genuinely surprised. He’d figured the ignorant servants were exaggerating, but these boys really did belong to an elite clan.

Their wide sleeves were tailored with an ethereal lightness, billowing gently with every shift. They carried themselves with an austere, untouchable grace—an unmistakable uniform of the Gusu Lan Sect. More importantly, these were blood descendants of the main family; tied neatly across each forehead was a pristine, finger-width white ribbon embroidered with a stylized cloud pattern.

The motto of the Gusu Lan Sect was “To be upright and righteous,” and that ribbon was meant to symbolize self-restraint. The rolling cloud motif was the family’s sacred crest. Outer disciples, guest elders, and affiliated cultivators wore blank ribbons with no crest allowed.

Just looking at a Lan gave Wei Wuxian phantom toothaches. In his previous life, he had constantly sneered at their uniform, calling it mourning robes for a funeral that hadn't happened yet. He could never mistake them.

Madam Mo hadn’t seen her nephew in years. It took her several seconds of stunned disbelief to recognize the garish clown standing in her parlor. Mortification flared into incandescent rage, though she fought to keep her voice down in front of company. Leaning toward her husband, she hissed through gritted teeth, “Who unlocked his door?! Drag him out of here!”

Her husband nodded frantically, wearing a sick look of dismay as he scrambled up to haul the boy away. But before his hands could find purchase, Wei Wuxian dropped flat onto his back. He splayed his arms and legs, practically suctioning himself to the stone floorboards. No matter how much the husband pushed, pulled, or dragged, Wei Wuxian didn’t budge an inch. Desperate, the man called in a few burly servants to help heave him out, but it was like trying to lift a boulder rooted in the mountain. If the guests weren't watching, the man would have booted the boy straight in the ribs. Under Madam Mo’s increasingly murderous glare, sweat broke out across his forehead. He snarled under his breath, “You crazy little bastard! Get back to your room before I make you regret it!”

The villagers knew Mo Xuanyu had lost his mind years ago, but he’d spent the last few locked away in the dark, out of sight. Watching him thrash about like a painted ghoul had the onlookers buzzing with delighted whispers. There was nothing the town loved more than high-society drama.

Wei Wuxian called out cheerily from the floor, “I’ll go back! Sure!” He raised an accusatory finger, pointing straight at Mo Ziyuan. “Just tell him to give me back the things he stole first.”

Mo Ziyuan went pale, then violently red. He never imagined this madman would have the audacity to make a scene here. He’d beaten him half to death yesterday, and here he was, airing dirty laundry in front of the immortals! “You're full of shit!” Mo Ziyuan blurted out. “When did I ever steal from you? Why the hell would I need to take your trash?!”

Wei Wuxian grinned. “Right, right, my bad! You didn't steal it—you robbed me!”

Madam Mo caught on immediately. Mo Xuanyu wasn't raving mad right now; he was lucid, deliberate, and bent on making them a laughingstock in front of the sect cultivators. Rage and panic clawed at her throat. “You came here on purpose to cause a scene, didn’t you?!”

Wei Wuxian blinked with faux innocence. “He robbed me blind, and I came to ask for my stuff back. How is that making a scene?”

Before Madam Mo could bite back, Mo Ziyuan lost his temper completely. He lunged forward, swinging a vicious kick aimed straight at Wei Wuxian's ribs. Across the room, the lead disciple in white flicked a slender finger. Mo Ziyuan’s balance instantly gave out under an invisible tug; his foot missed entirely, sending him skidding awkwardly onto his backside.

Wei Wuxian seized the cue, rolling dramatically across the floor like he’d taken a devastating blow. In the process, he pulled his collar wide, exposing his bare chest—and right smack in the center sat the purpling, unmistakable boot-print from yesterday's beating.

The gossiping crowd gasped in unison, thoroughly entertained. Mo Xuanyu couldn't have stamped a boot-print onto his own chest at that angle. No matter how broken his mind was, he still carried Mo blood! To beat their own kin black and blue like that… The boy had been eccentric when he returned, sure, but he hadn't been completely mad. Ten to one, this abusive household had driven him over the edge. Regardless of who was right, this public spectacle beat watching a cultivation exhibition any day of the week!

With dozens of villagers whispering and pointing, Madam Mo couldn't lay a hand on him, nor could she throw him out without looking guilty. Swallowing her bile, she smoothed her skirts and tried to force a dismissive smile. “Stealing? Robbery? What ugly words to use between family. He merely borrowed a few curiosities to study them. A-Yuan is your younger cousin—what harm is there in sharing? As the elder brother, must you really be so petty over child’s play? Throwing a tantrum and making a fool of yourself in public, as if we wouldn’t return them.”

The Lan disciples exchanged baffled glances. One of the boys taking a sip of tea almost sprayed it across the table. Raised under the strict, pristine mountain air of Cloud Recesses, these boys had grown up surrounded by refined arts and unyielding virtue; they had clearly never witnessed a family brawl this trashy, nor heard logic this brazenly backwards. Today was proving quite the education.

Wei Wuxian practically laughed aloud. He sat up and shoved out an open palm. “Great! Give them back then.”

Mo Ziyuan couldn't give them back even if he wanted to. Half the talismans were shredded, the trinkets were smashed, and the rest were long gone. Even if he had them intact, he’d rather die than humble himself. Veins bulging on his neck, he choked out, “Mother!” His glare practically screamed: Are you really going to let this freak humiliate me?!

Madam Mo shot him a venomous warning glare, silently telling him to shut up before he ruined things further.

Undeterred, Wei Wuxian drove the dagger deeper. “And while we’re on the subject, not only should he keep his sticky fingers off my things, but he definitely shouldn't be sneaking into my room in the dead of night to do it. Everyone knows I prefer men. He might not have any shame, but I have a reputation to protect. You know how people talk!”

Madam Mo gasped in sheer horror, shrieking, “Listen to the filth coming out of your mouth in front of our elders! Shameless degenerate! A-Yuan is your own cousin!”

When it came to making a scene, Wei Wuxian was a certified master. In his previous life, he’d always kept a sliver of aristocratic decorum to avoid humiliating his clan, but right now? He was an unhinged madman! Dignity was completely off the table. He leaned his head back and hollered with pristine, shameless indignity: “He knew damn well he’s my cousin, yet he still crawled into my bedroom without a shred of boundary! Who’s the real shameless one here?! You might not care about your son's purity, but don’t you dare ruin my virtue! I still need to marry a good man someday!!!”

Mo Ziyuan let out an animalistic roar. Snatching up a heavy wooden chair, he swung it overhead to cave the freak’s skull in.

Finally cracked. Wei Wuxian scrambled up like an oiled eel, ducking clear. The heavy chair shattered against the stone flagstones with an ear-splitting crash. The townspeople who had been happily snickering at the family’s disgrace suddenly scattered like frightened birds, dodging flying splinters so they wouldn’t catch a stray bruise.

Wei Wuxian bolted straight toward the bewildered Lan disciples, ducking behind their robes and squawking at the crowd, “You all saw it! Did you see that?! The thief is resorting to murder! Where is the justice?!”

Mo Ziyuan lunged to throttle him, but the lead Lan disciple stepped smoothly into his path, his voice firm yet measured. “Young Master Mo… please, compose yourself. Let us speak reasonably.”

Madam Mo saw the young cultivator shielding the madman and felt her heart sink. Forcing a strained, tremulous smile, she said, “Young Master, that boy is my late sister’s son. He’s… unwell in the head. Everyone in Mo Village knows he's completely mad. He spouts wild nonsense constantly; none of it can be taken seriously. Please, immortals, do not take offense…”

Before she could finish, Wei Wuxian poked his powdered face out from behind the disciple's shoulder. “Who says I'm talking nonsense? Anyone who dares touch my stuff again can test me—steal from me once, and I’ll chop off your damn hand!”

Mo Ziyuan, held back by his father, violently surged again at the threat. Wei Wuxian didn’t stick around to chat; he sang a merry, mocking tune and slipped through the crowd like a greased fish.

The lead Lan disciple moved to block the doorway, cutting off pursuit and deftly steering the conversation back to serious matters with a deadpan, professional tone: “Ahem… as discussed, we will be borrowing your Western Courtyard for tonight. Please keep in mind what I explained earlier: once dusk falls, bolt your doors and windows tight. Do not wander outside, and under no circumstances should anyone approach that courtyard.”

Madam Mo was trembling with bottled fury, but blocked by the cultivator, she could only grit her teeth and bow stiffly. “Yes, yes… We are in your debt, young immortals…”

Mo Ziyuan gaped in raw disbelief. “Mother! That lunatic slandered me in front of the whole town, and we're just letting him walk?! You promised me! You said he was just a—”

“Shut your mouth!” Madam Mo hissed. “Whatever you have to say, keep it until we are behind closed doors!”

Mo Ziyuan had never swallowed such humiliation in his life, nor had he ever been publicly reined in by his mother. He stared out the doorway, trembling with pure venom, and muttered under his breath, “That bastard is dead tonight!”

Having sufficiently made a fool of himself, Wei Wuxian strolled out the main gates and took a leisurely victory lap through Mo Village. He horrified half the townsfolk along the way, but found himself thoroughly enjoying the perks of being a local madman. He even grew rather fond of the grotesque hanging-ghost makeup, deciding it was too much hassle to wash off anyway. Besides, there's no water in that hovel, so why bother?

He smoothed down his hair and glanced at his wrists. The jagged, bloody slash marks hadn't faded in the slightest.

Which meant merely throwing a public tantrum and embarrassing the family wasn't nearly enough to appease Mo Xuanyu’s vendetta.

Did the kid really want him to slaughter the entire Mo clan?

…Honestly, that wouldn't be very difficult.

Mulling it over, Wei Wuxian drifted back toward the Mo manor. As he tip-toed past the Western Courtyard, he noticed the Lan disciples perched across the rooftops and high perimeter walls, conversing in hushed, serious tones. Curious, he tiptoed back and stood near the wall, staring up at them with a vacant, wide-eyed look.

The Gusu Lan Sect had played a massive part in the siege that ended his life, but these kids hadn't even been born back then—or were barely toddling around in short robes. He held no grudge against the younger generation. He was simply curious to see how the new kids handled night-hunts.

As he watched them work, his eyes narrowed.

Wait a minute…

Why did those black banners fluttering on the roof ridges look so damn familiar?

Those were Spirit Attraction Flags. When pinned onto a living person, they acted as a beacon, luring every nearby resentful spirit, malicious ghost, walking corpse, and dark entity straight toward the bearer. Because whoever wore one was essentially transformed into a living target, people also dubbed them "Target Flags." They could be planted on buildings too, so long as living bait remained inside, expanding the slaughter zone to include everyone under that roof. And because resentful energy always swirled around them like a shadowy gale, they were colloquially known as "Black Wind Flags."

Setting up a perimeter of flags in the Western Courtyard and forbidding anyone from approaching meant these disciples were intending to funnel all the rogue walking corpses into one contained ring and exterminate them in one fell swoop.

And as for why they looked familiar… of course they did. The creator of the Spirit Attraction Flag was none other than the Yiling Laozu himself!

It seemed that while the entire cultivation world bayed for his blood, they had zero qualms about continuing to use his inventions.

A disciple standing along the eaves caught sight of him gawking and called down, “Go on home. This isn’t a place for you.”

Though dismissive, the tone was polite and genuinely concerned—a night-and-day contrast from the manor servants. Catching the boy off guard, Wei Wuxian bounded up onto the wall and snatched one of the flags clean from the brickwork.

The disciple flinched in shock, dropping down from the ridge to give chase. “Don’t touch that! Put it back, it’s dangerous!”

Wei Wuxian sprinted around the yard, his hair whipping wild as he waved his arms like a manic toddler. “Not giving it back! It's mine! I want it!”

The Lan disciple caught him in two strides, snagging his sleeve. “Are you going to give that back or do I have to make you?”

Wei Wuxian clutched the flag to his chest like a prized toy. Drawn by the scuffle, the lead disciple drifted down lightly from the roof, his boots barely making a sound on the pavers. “Jingyi, leave it. Just ask him for it nicely; there’s no need to rough him up.”

Lan Jingyi huffed, “Sizhui, I wasn’t going to hit him! But look at him, he completely ruined the flag formation!”

During the scuffle, Wei Wuxian had already given the stolen banner a thorough inspection. The ink strokes were accurate, the incantations were complete, and the core talisman had no structural errors. It would work fine. The only issue was the draftsman’s lack of experience; the energy resonance would only draw spirits within a five-mile radius. Still, for a backwater town like Mo Village, that was more than enough.

Lan Sizhui offered him a gentle, patient smile. “Young Master Mo, dusk is setting in, and we’re about to lure the corpses here. It won't be safe outside. Please head back to your quarters.”

Wei Wuxian took a good look at the boy. Refined, composed, handsome, with a gentle calm lingering at the corners of his lips—a genuinely exceptional seedling. Setting aside his tidy formation work, his manners were impeccable. Wei Wuxian found himself wondering who in that stiff, conservative sect of walking rulebooks could possibly raise such a well-adjusted kid.

Lan Sizhui reached out gently. “May I have the flag back…?”

Before the boy could finish, Wei Wuxian tossed the banner carelessly onto the dirt, turning up his nose. “It's just a ragged piece of cloth! You think you’re so special? I can draw way better ones than this!”

He turned and bolted, laughing into the wind. Up on the eaves, a couple of disciples nearly lost their footing from laughing at his outrageous boasting. Lan Jingyi shook his head in half-amused exasperation as he retrieved the banner and dusted it off. “Total lunatic.”

Lan Sizhui said softly, “Be kind. Come on, we need to finish the array.”

Meanwhile, Wei Wuxian spent the rest of the evening wandering aimlessly through the estate before ambling back to Mo Xuanyu’s cramped room. The door bolt was splintered, and the wrecked furniture remained scattered across the dirt. Ignoring the mess, he found a relatively clean patch of floor and sank back into meditation.

He didn't make it to sunrise.

A chaotic wave of noise ripped him right out of his trance.

Frantic footsteps, panicked screams, and raw sobbing tore through the quiet night, closing in fast on his door. Wei Wuxian could hear frantic voices shouting over one another:

“…Kick it open and drag him out!”

“Call the magistrates!”

“To hell with the magistrates—beat the bastard to death right now!”

His eyes snapped open just as several servants kicked the splintered door inward. Torches painted the small courtyard in roaring orange light, and a harsh voice bellowed:

“Drag this murderous psycho to the main hall and make him pay with his life!”
